title: What happens to abandoned mines?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore abandoned mines: how many exist in the United States (estimates of roughly 300,000 to 500,000, with only about 31,000 located by the Bureau of Land Management as of February 2011), the physical dangers (drownings in flooded quarries and shafts, falls, cave-ins, carbon monoxide and asphyxiation) and environmental hazards (acid mine drainage, acid groundwater, mercury tailings from gold mining). They discuss why companies abandoned sites, how bankruptcy and lost records left no one liable, the 1997 bonding requirement, the Clean Water Act exemption legislation, the cost of cleanup (about $72 billion for hard rock mines per 2006 testimony), BLM's Abandoned Mine Lands program and its funding, sealing shafts while protecting bat populations with bat gates, the Superfund and abandoned mine reclamation fund coal tax, and the Department of Interior's mining excellence award. The episode closes with listener mail, including a question about cilantro and news of Andy Griffith's death.

segments.title: Opening banter and Taylor Crane mine death
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter, then Josh recounts the death of sixteen-year-old Taylor Crane, who fell into a thousand-foot abandoned mine shaft during a tour of abandoned haciendas and mines in Mexico.

segments.title: How many abandoned mines and deaths
segments.summary: They estimate the US has roughly 300,000 to 500,000 abandoned mines and that about thirty people die each year in accidents involving them, mostly drownings in quarries and flooded shafts, with carbon monoxide and asphyxiation also cited. Since 2001, 27 deaths are mentioned.

segments.title: Physical hazards and glory holes
segments.summary: They discuss physical hazards such as falling or cave-ins, the term glory holes for depressions from mine collapses, and mine tailings that can be toxic and run off into water.

segments.title: Environmental hazards: acid drainage and mercury
segments.summary: The hosts describe acid groundwater produced when sulfide minerals meet oxygen and water, acid rain from mines, and mercury used in gold amalgamation that contaminates areas where it is burned off.

segments.title: Why companies abandoned mines and liability loopholes
segments.summary: Chuck asks why companies don't clean up. Josh says cost is the main reason and that before 1997 companies could simply walk away. Lost land and lease records, and bankruptcy shielding owners, left no one liable; the hosts note a later bonding requirement for mining companies that is meant to fund reclamation.

segments.title: Clean Water Act exemption and cleanup methods
segments.summary: They discuss a 2006 proposed exemption from the Clean Water Act for people cleaning up mines, which did not pass, and critics like Earthworks who said it was too broad. BLM's Abandoned Mine Lands division often builds structures around sites, compared to Chernobyl.

segments.title: Funding, bat gates, and Superfund
segments.summary: BLM's Abandoned Mine Lands program gets about twelve to fifteen million dollars a year and cleaned over three thousand mines in eight years. Sealing shafts can disturb bats, so bat gates let bats in and out while keeping people out. The EPA's Superfund and a coal per-ton tax fund reclamation.

segments.title: Responsible mining and reclamation awards
segments.summary: The hosts note that many modern miners reclaim land, and the Department of the Interior has a mining excellence award. They urge listeners to stay away from abandoned mines and to report them.

segments.title: Show plugs and search bar
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh close the mine discussion, pointing listeners to the website search bar for more on abandoned mines.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener questions cover soup versus stew, a Judge John Hodge podcast plug, Andy Griffith's death, an anniversary shout-out, a would-you-rather question, Atlanta, and why cilantro divides people. Contact information is given and the episode ends.
